claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is among the most successful human pathogens and forms long-term, chronic infections that can span decades.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is among the most successful human pathogens and forms long-term, chronic infections that can span decades.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of Mtb infections, drawing from established scientific knowledge about tuberculosis pathogenesis.

claim: Macrophages are central to tuberculosis pathogenesis as they are both the major site of Mtb replication yet also trigger antimicrobial functions required for host resistance to infection.
source: Macrophages are central to tuberculosis pathogenesis as they are both the major site of Mtb replication yet also trigger antimicrobial functions required for host resistance to infection (Russell, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Russell, 2011, indicating it draws from published literature.

claim: The intimate interactions between Mtb and macrophages have coevolved over nearly 70,000 years.
source: Uncovering these intimate interactions, which have coevolved over nearly 70,000 years (Comas et al., 2013), may reveal novel therapeutic intervention strategies to treat the nearly ten million people who fall ill to tuberculosis infection each year (World Health Organization, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Comas et al., 2013.

claim: Nearly ten million people fall ill to tuberculosis infection each year.
source: Uncovering these intimate interactions, which have coevolved over nearly 70,000 years (Comas et al., 2013), may reveal novel therapeutic intervention strategies to treat the nearly ten million people who fall ill to tuberculosis infection each year (World Health Organization, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization, 2018.

claim: Mtb infection of macrophages engages several pattern recognition receptors including toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) leading to expression of inflammatory mediators.
source: Mtb infection of macrophages engages several pattern recognition receptors including toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) leading to expression of inflammatory mediators (Gopalakrishnan and Salgame, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gopalakrishnan and Salgame, 2016.

claim: After phagocytosis, the bacterial-containing phagosome enters into the canonical endosomal/lysosomal pathway, which is under the control of Rab GTPases, including Rab5 and Rab7.
source: After phagocytosis, the bacterial-containing phagosome enters into the canonical endosomal/lysosomal pathway, which is under the control of Rab GTPases, including Rab5 and Rab7.
evidence: This is a statement about cellular trafficking pathways, drawing from established knowledge about endosomal biology.

claim: The typical maturation of the Mtb-containing phagosome is actively blocked by Mtb and fails to acidify or acquire markers of late endosomes/lysosomes.
source: However, the typical maturation of this compartment is actively blocked by Mtb and fails to acidify or acquire markers of late endosomes/lysosomes (Sturgill-Koszycki et al., 1994), an activity observed in early electron microscopy studies (Armstrong and Hart, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sturgill-Koszycki et al., 1994 and Armstrong and Hart, 1971.

claim: The effect of virulent Mtb on host intracellular vesicle trafficking requires the type VII protein secretion system ESX-1.
source: While this effect of virulent Mtb on host intracellular vesicle trafficking requires the type VII protein secretion system ESX-1 (MacGurn and Cox, 2007), the mechanism of phagosomal maturation arrest remains mysterious.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to MacGurn and Cox, 2007.

claim: The mechanism of phagosomal maturation arrest remains mysterious.
source: While this effect of virulent Mtb on host intracellular vesicle trafficking requires the type VII protein secretion system ESX-1 (MacGurn and Cox, 2007), the mechanism of phagosomal maturation arrest remains mysterious.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, indicating a gap in understanding.

claim: The ESX-1 system mediates limited perforation of the phagosomal membrane.
source: Importantly, the ESX-1 system mediates limited perforation of the phagosomal membrane, which in turn activates two cytosolic pathways in host cells (Watson et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2012; Manzanillo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Watson et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2012; Manzanillo et al., 2012.

claim: ESX-1-mediated phagosomal membrane perforation activates the cGAS/STING/TBK1 signal transduction cascade leading to production of type I IFN and a profound antiviral transcriptional response that inhibits host resistance.
source: First, activation of the cGAS/STING/TBK1 signal transduction cascade leads to production of type I IFN and a profound antiviral transcriptional response that inhibits host resistance (Watson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Watson et al., 2015.

claim: Cytosolic access by Mtb activates ubiquitin-mediated selective autophagy targeting, an evolutionary ancient anti-microbial cellular response that counteracts phagosome maturation arrest by actively targeting microbes to lysosomes.
source: Second, cytosolic access by Mtb also activates ubiquitin-mediated selective autophagy targeting, an evolutionary ancient anti-microbial cellular response that counteracts phagosome maturation arrest by actively targeting microbes to lysosomes (Via et al., 1997; Choy and Roy, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Via et al., 1997 and Choy and Roy, 2013.

claim: Some components of the host autophagic machinery are critical for controlling infection.
source: Although some components of the host autophagic machinery are critical for controlling infection (Watson et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2009), it remains unclear whether this antimicrobial effect is dependent on canonical autophagy (Kimmey et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Watson et al., 2012 and Zheng et al., 2009.

claim: It remains unclear whether the antimicrobial effect of autophagy is dependent on canonical autophagy.
source: Although some components of the host autophagic machinery are critical for controlling infection (Watson et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2009), it remains unclear whether this antimicrobial effect is dependent on canonical autophagy (Kimmey et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimmey et al., 2015, indicating ongoing uncertainty in the field.

claim: Global, unbiased approaches to probe the Mtb-macrophage interface have primarily relied on measuring changes in mRNA levels.
source: Global, unbiased approaches to probe the Mtb-macrophage interface have primarily relied on measuring changes in mRNA levels that, while facile, naturally limit the analysis of cellular state toward signal transduction cascades that directly lead to transcriptional outputs (Ehrt et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ehrt et al., 2001.

claim: Monitoring changes in protein post-translational modifications (PTMs) represents a more comprehensive way to assess changes in cellular state during infection than measuring mRNA levels.
source: While these studies have certainly uncovered insights into the mechanisms of Mtb pathogenesis (Ehrt et al., 2001; Berry et al., 2010), monitoring changes in protein post-translational modifications (PTMs) represents a more comprehensive way to assess changes in cellular state during infection, as essentially all cell biological pathways, including intracellular trafficking, autophagy, nuclear import, and metabolism are regulated by PTMs.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of PTM analysis, drawing from established knowledge about cellular regulation and supported by inference from the limitations of mRNA analysis.

claim: Many intracellular bacterial pathogens hijack or alter normal PTMs of host proteins to manipulate cells and promote their pathogenesis.
source: Indeed, many intracellular bacterial pathogens hijack or alter normal PTMs of host proteins to manipulate cells and promote their pathogenesis (Roy and Mukherjee, 2009; Patel et al., 2009; Fiskin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Roy and Mukherjee, 2009; Patel et al., 2009; Fiskin et al., 2016.

claim: Selective autophagy is predominantly regulated by PTMs rather than transcription.
source: Selective autophagy is predominantly regulated by PTMs rather than transcription (Lamark et al., 2017), as it is under the control of several types of modification, especially ubiquitylation and phosphorylation (Herhaus and Dikic, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lamark et al., 2017 and Herhaus and Dikic, 2015.

claim: Initial targeting of intracellular structures to autophagy is mediated by ubiquitylation of the cargo.
source: Initial targeting of intracellular structures (intracellular pathogens, damaged organelles, protein aggregates, etc.) to autophagy is mediated by ubiquitylation of the cargo.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of selective autophagy, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Autophagy receptors recognize ubiquitin signals and recruit phagophore membranes to the cargo via interactions with LC3/GABARAP proteins.
source: Autophagy receptors then recognize these ubiquitin signals and recruit phagophore membranes to the cargo via interactions with LC3/GABARAP proteins embedded in these vesicles, ultimately enveloping cargo inside a continuous autophagic vacuole competent for fusion with lysosomes.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of selective autophagy, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Ubiquitylation of p62 and phosphorylation of Optineurin increase their activity upon recruitment to cargo, forming a positive feedback loop promoting autophagosome completion.
source: For example, ubiquitylation of p62 and phosphorylation of Optineurin increase their activity upon recruitment to cargo, forming a positive feedback loop promoting autophagosome completion (Peng et al., 2017; Matsumoto et al., 2011; Heo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peng et al., 2017; Matsumoto et al., 2011; Heo et al., 2015.

claim: Some ubiquitin ligases required for selective autophagy of Mtb have been identified.
source: In the case of Mtb, some ubiquitin ligases required for selective autophagy have been identified (Manzanillo et al., 2013; Franco et al., 2017), but their substrates and roles are still mysterious and other ubiquitin ligases are likely required.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Manzanillo et al., 2013 and Franco et al., 2017.

claim: Some autophagy receptors have been implicated in autophagy of the Mtb-containing vacuole.
source: Likewise, some autophagy receptors have been implicated in autophagy of the Mtb-containing vacuole (Watson et al., 2012; Manzanillo et al., 2013; Franco et al., 2017), but many have not been tested (Rogov et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Watson et al., 2012; Manzanillo et al., 2013; Franco et al., 2017.

claim: The study used mass spectrometry to comprehensively identify changes in host protein abundance, phosphorylation, and ubiquitylation during a 24 hr time course of primary murine macrophages infected with virulent Mtb.
source: Here, we report our findings using mass spectrometry (MS) to comprehensively identify changes in host protein abundance, phosphorylation, and ubiquitylation during a 24 hr time course of primary murine macrophages infected with virulent Mtb.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The study identified hundreds of dynamically regulated phosphorylation and ubiquitylation sites during Mtb infection.
source: We identified hundreds of dynamically regulated phosphorylation and ubiquitylation sites, indicating that dramatic remodeling of multiple host pathways, both expected and unexpected, occurred during infection.
evidence: This claim is based on the mass spectrometry data generated in the study.

claim: Most of the cellular changes during Mtb infection were not captured by mRNA profiling.
source: Most of these cellular changes were not captured by mRNA profiling, and included activation of ubiquitin-mediated autophagy, an evolutionarily ancient cellular antimicrobial system.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the proteomic data with transcriptomic data, as shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The analysis revealed that TAX1BP1 mediates clearance of ubiquitylated Mtb and targets bacteria to LC3-positive phagophores.
source: This analysis also revealed that a particular autophagy receptor, TAX1BP1, mediates clearance of ubiquitylated Mtb and targets bacteria to LC3-positive phagophores.
evidence: This claim is based on the genetic and microscopy experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Primary murine bone-marrow-derived macrophages were infected with Mtb in biological triplicate and harvested at 2-, 4-, 6-, 8-, and 24 hr post-infection.
source: To this end, we infected primary murine bone-marrow-derived macrophages with Mtb in biological triplicate, harvested infected cells at 2-, 4-, 6-, 8-, and 24 hr post-infection, and prepared protein lysates (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Time-matched mock infections were performed at 0 hr, 6 hr, and 24 hr time points.
source: We also performed time-matched mock infections of the same macrophages harvested at an early (0 hr), middle (6 hr), or late (24 hr) time points.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Extremely few changes were identified between uninfected cells at all three time points (0, 6, and 24 hr).
source: Because we identified extremely few changes between uninfected cells at all three time points, we simply matched the Mtb-infected cell data from the 2- and 4 hr time points with the data from the 0 hr mock sample, and the 6- and 8 hr time points with the data from the 6 hr mock sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Pair-wise comparison of parent ion MS intensity measurements between technical and biological replicates from the same condition were highly reproducible.
source: Pair-wise comparison of parent ion MS intensity measurements between technical and biological replicates from the same condition were highly reproducible, as indicated by strong correlation coefficients from global abundance, phospho-enriched, or diGly-enriched samples (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Over 1000 statistically significant changes in abundance or PTMs were identified during Mtb infection.
source: Comparison of peptide levels in Mtb infected samples versus uninfected controls revealed over 1000 statistically significant changes in abundance or PTMs during Mtb infection (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3; Figure 2C-G), indicating pronounced changes to the macrophage proteome.
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3 and Figure 2C-G.

claim: The number of statistically significant changes in protein abundance or ubiquitylation progressively increased over the time course.
source: The number of statistically significant changes in protein abundance or ubiquitylation progressively increased over the time course (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Phosphopeptide changes were bimodal with the greatest number of changes occurring early (2- or 4 hr post-infection) or late (24 hr) after Mtb infection.
source: In contrast, phosphopeptide changes were bimodal with the greatest number of phosphopeptide changes occurring early (2- or 4 hr post-infection) or late (24 hr) after Mtb infection (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At 6 hr post-infection, there was weak correlation (ρ = 0.36) between relative protein and RNA abundance.
source: Overall, our data is consistent with previous findings of dendritic cells treated with LPS (Berg-Larsen et al., 2013), as we observed weak correlation between relative protein and RNA abundance early after infection (6 hr time point, Pearson coefficient ρ = 0.36, Figure 1—figure supplement 4), but at 24 hr post-infection the correlation was much stronger (ρ = 0.74, Figure 1D) indicating that by this time point the changes in the proteome are largely reflective of changes in the transcriptome.
evidence: This claim is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and is supported by citation to Berg-Larsen et al., 2013.

claim: At 24 hr post-infection, the correlation between relative protein and RNA abundance was much stronger (ρ = 0.74).
source: Overall, our data is consistent with previous findings of dendritic cells treated with LPS (Berg-Larsen et al., 2013), as we observed weak correlation between relative protein and RNA abundance early after infection (6 hr time point, Pearson coefficient ρ = 0.36, Figure 1—figure supplement 4), but at 24 hr post-infection the correlation was much stronger (ρ = 0.74, Figure 1D) indicating that by this time point the changes in the proteome are largely reflective of changes in the transcriptome.
evidence: This claim is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Poor correlations were observed between relative changes in mRNA compared to changes in phosphorylated (ρ = 0.37) or ubiquitylated proteins (ρ = 0.52) at 24 hr post-infection.
source: Interestingly, we observed poor correlations between relative changes in mRNA compared to changes in phosphorylated (ρ = 0.37, Figure 1E) or ubiquitylated proteins (ρ = 0.52, Figure 1F) at this same late time point.
evidence: This claim is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Changes in RNA abundance is a moderate predictor for changes in protein abundance in response to infection, but other biological processes controlled by PTMs are at play during macrophage infection.
source: Thus, these results suggest that while changes in RNA abundance is a moderate predictor for changes in protein abundance in response to infection, other biological process controlled by PTMs are at play during macrophage infection, reinforcing the notion that proteomics is a valuable method to identify biological processes during infection that are independent of gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: 470 proteins changed significantly in abundance during Mtb infection.
source: A comparison of individual proteins that changed significantly in abundance (n = 470), phosphorylation (n = 1489), or ubiquitylation (n = 606) during Mtb infection, indicated limited overlap between the three categories (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 1489 proteins changed significantly in phosphorylation during Mtb infection.
source: A comparison of individual proteins that changed significantly in abundance (n = 470), phosphorylation (n = 1489), or ubiquitylation (n = 606) during Mtb infection, indicated limited overlap between the three categories (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 606 proteins changed significantly in ubiquitylation during Mtb infection.
source: A comparison of individual proteins that changed significantly in abundance (n = 470), phosphorylation (n = 1489), or ubiquitylation (n = 606) during Mtb infection, indicated limited overlap between the three categories (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was limited overlap between proteins that changed in abundance, phosphorylation, or ubiquitylation during Mtb infection.
source: A comparison of individual proteins that changed significantly in abundance (n = 470), phosphorylation (n = 1489), or ubiquitylation (n = 606) during Mtb infection, indicated limited overlap between the three categories (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on the Venn diagram shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Antiviral responses were highly enriched in the global abundance dataset (p=4.53×10−20).
source: As expected based on previous literature, antiviral responses were highly enriched (p=4.53×10−20 in the global abundance dataset; Figure 3C), including response to type I (IFN-β p=4.25×10−16, and IFN-α 3.81 × 10−10 in the global abundance dataset; Figure 3C), likely due to phagosome perforation and activation of the cGAS/STING/TBK1 pathway (Flynn et al., 1993; Cooper et al., 1993; Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C, and is supported by citations to Flynn et al., 1993; Cooper et al., 1993; Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2018.

claim: Small GTPase mediated signal transduction was highly enriched in the phosphopeptide datasets (p=2.12×10−26).
source: Small GTPase mediated signal transduction was also highly enriched in the phosphopeptide datasets, which included Rab GTPases (Rab7, 8b, and 14), guanine nucleotide exchange factors (RabGef1, ArfGef1-2, ArhGef2, Dock1, 2, 5, 8, and 11), and GTPase activators (ArfGap 1, 2, 3, 12, 17, 18, 24, 25, 30, 35) (p=2.12×10−26; Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Enrichment of proteins in the category 'regulation of catabolic processes' (p=2.39×10−25) was identified in the phosphopeptide dataset.
source: We identified an enrichment in modified proteins in the category 'regulation of catabolic processes' (p=2.39×10−25 in the phosphopeptide dataset; Figure 3C), which includes components of the autophagy machinery such as Atg4b, Rubicon, autophagy kinases (Ulk1, Ulk2), and autophagy receptors (Optineurin, Bnip3l).
evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Enriched functional pathways not previously implicated in Mtb pathogenesis include nucleocytoplasmic transport (p=1.92×10−19) and response to DNA damage (p=2.08×10−18).
source: We identified other enriched functional pathways not previously implicated in Mtb pathogenesis such as nucleocytoplasmic transport and response to DNA damage (p=1.92×10−19, p=2.08×10−18; Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Protein abundance changes clustered into two large groups and several smaller clusters.
source: Protein abundance changes clustered into two large groups and several smaller clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on the cluster analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The group of proteins that increased in abundance during Mtb infection was functionally enriched for inflammatory, antiviral, and 'response to bacterium' pathways.
source: The group of proteins that increased in abundance during Mtb infection was functionally enriched for inflammatory, antiviral, and 'response to bacterium', suggestive they are predominantly targets of TLR signaling (i.e., TLR2, NOS2, Il1b, FCGR4; Figure 3—figure supplement 2; p=2.19×10−13, 2.51 × 10−25, 8.32 × 10−15).
evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: OASL1 had the fourth greatest fold change among all non-imputed proteins that changed in abundance (34-fold change, p=1.56×10−12).
source: Strikingly, among all of the non-imputed proteins that changed in abundance, OASL1 had the fourth greatest fold change (Figure 3A; 34-fold change, p=1.56×10−12), and there was also a large increase in OASL1 mRNA at the same time point (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 1D.

claim: Murine OASL1 downregulates the type I IFN response by binding to and inhibiting translation of IRF7 mRNA.
source: While OAS proteins activate cleavage of viral nucleic acid (Choi et al., 2015), murine OASL1 downregulates the type I IFN response by binding to and inhibiting translation of IRF7 mRNA (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2015 and Lee et al., 2013.

claim: OASL1 mRNA was increased in macrophages infected with a hypervirulent Mtb strain.
source: OASL1 regulation of the type I IFN response may play a critical role in Mtb pathogenesis as OASL1 mRNA was recently described to be increased in macrophages infected with a hypervirulent Mtb strain (Leisching et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leisching et al., 2017.

claim: The second cluster of proteins decreased in abundance and included ribosome biogenesis and DNA replication pathways (p=8.92×10−10, 8.32 × 10−11).
source: The second cluster of proteins decreased in abundance and included ribosome biogenesis and DNA replication pathways (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; p=8.92×10−10, 8.32 × 10−11), consistent with studies indicating that Mtb infection may arrest macrophage growth (Cumming et al., 2017), a strategy utilized by the intracellular pathogen Legionella pneumophila (Moss et al., 2019; Sol et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and is supported by citations to Cumming et al., 2017; Moss et al., 2019; Sol et al., 2019.

claim: There was a statistically significant increase in the autophagy receptors p62 and TAX1BP1 during Mtb infection.
source: Although the autophagy pathway was not significantly enriched in our abundance data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), there was a statistically significant increase in the autophagy receptors p62 and TAX1BP1 during Mtb infection (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Ubiquitylated substrates clustered into four classes during the 24 hr time course.
source: During the 24 hr time course, ubiquitylated substrates clustered into four classes: 1. Peptides that decreased in ubiquitylation during infection, 2. Peptides that had increased ubiquitylation early (2–4 hr) after infection, 3. Peptides that were ubiquitylated between 6–8 hr after infection, and 4. Peptides that were identified as ubiquitylated only at the 24 hr time point (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is based on the cluster analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Autophagy was enriched at the later time points of infection (class 3 and 4).
source: Autophagy, for example, was enriched at the later time points of infection (class 3 and 4; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: An enrichment in histones was identified among the group of proteins with decreased ubiquitylation during Mtb infection (Class 1, p=1.82×10−7, 5.89 × 10−7).
source: We also identified an enrichment in histones among the group of proteins with decreased ubiquitylation during Mtb infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Class 1, p=1.82×10−7, 5.89 × 10−7), which is likely reflective of the dramatic changes in the transcriptional program of macrophages when they encounter bacteria (Zou and Mallampalli, 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3, and is supported by a citation to Zou and Mallampalli, 2014.

claim: Phosphorylated substrates clustered into four discrete classes.
source: Phosphorylated substrates also clustered together into four discrete classes: 1. Proteins that increased early after infection, 2. Proteins that increased later after infection, 3. Proteins that decreased early after infection, and 4. Proteins that decreased late after infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the cluster analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Actin cytoskeleton organization and small GTPase mediated signal transduction changed dramatically throughout the 24 hr time course of infection as they were significantly enriched in all of the phosphorylation clusters.
source: This analysis revealed that actin cytoskeleton organization and small GTPase mediated signal transduction changed dramatically throughout the 24 hr time course of infection as they were significantly enriched in all of the clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PhosFate bioinformatic tool identified kinases expected to be activated during Mtb infection, including those involved in inflammatory (IKBKB) and stress responses (several MAP kinases) as well as type I IFN signaling (JAK/STATs).
source: Importantly, this approach identified kinases expected to be activated during Mtb infection, including those involved in inflammatory (IKBKB) and stress responses (several MAP kinases) as well as type I IFN signaling (JAK/STATs).
evidence: This claim is based on the PhosFate analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Potential decreased activity of several cyclin dependent kinases was noted, consistent with the finding that primary macrophages stop proliferating upon infection.
source: Conversely, we also noted potential decreased activity of several cyclin dependent kinases, consistent with the finding that primary macrophages stop proliferating upon infection (Cumming et al., 2017; Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on the PhosFate analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, and is supported by a citation to Cumming et al., 2017.

claim: The autophagy pathway was prominently enriched in both PTM datasets.
source: The autophagy pathway was prominently enriched in both PTM datasets (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), with a significant number of phosphorylation events that occurred on autophagy cargo receptors (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3, and the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Among the autophagy receptors, p62 had the greatest number of phosphorylated residues that changed during Mtb infection and was among the most highly modified proteins in the proteomics datasets.
source: While both p62 and NDP52 have been linked to Mtb targeting to the autophagosome (Watson et al., 2012), we found that only p62 was modified. In fact, among the autophagy receptors, p62 had the greatest number of phosphorylated residues that changed during Mtb infection and was among the most highly modified proteins in our proteomics datasets.
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2A and is supported by a citation to Watson et al., 2012.

claim: Novel p62 phosphosites were identified at Ser-28, Ser-320, and Ser-372.
source: We identified many of the previously recognized p62 phosphosites, including Ser-152 in the RIPK1 domain and Ser-226 in the TRAF6-binding domain (Richter et al., 2016), but we have identified novel residues as well (Ser-28, Ser-320, Ser-372; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2B, and is supported by a citation to Richter et al., 2016.

claim: Four autophagy receptors (BNIP3L, Optineurin, FUNDC1, and TAX1BP1) were selectively modified upon Mtb infection.
source: Four receptors (BNIP3L, Optineurin, FUNDC1, and TAX1BP1) were selectively modified upon Mtb infection; these modifications occurred in functional domains of these receptors (Figure 2B) and changed through the time course of infection (Figure 2A,C–G).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and 2C-G.

claim: Colocalization of Mtb with NBR1, Optineurin, TAX1BP1 and p62 was detected.
source: Importantly, we detected colocalization of Mtb with NBR1, Optineurin, TAX1BP1 and p62 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on the microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both NBR1 and TAX1BP1 localized to Mtb to a similar extent as p62, whereas colocalization with Optineurin was considerably less frequent.
source: Quantification of the percent of Mtb-containing phagosomes that colocalized with each receptor revealed that both NBR1 and TAX1BP1 localized to a similar extent as p62, whereas colocalization with Optineurin was considerably less frequent.
evidence: This claim is based on the quantification shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The ~30% colocalization rate of Mtb with p62 is consistent with previous findings.
source: The ~30% colocalization rate of Mtb with p62 is consistent with previous findings (Watson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on the quantification shown in Figure 4B and is supported by a citation to Watson et al., 2012.

claim: Infected Tax1bp1-/- cells gave rise to significant increases in Mtb colocalization with ubiquitin, phospho-TBK1, and p62 compared to infected wild-type macrophages.
source: In contrast, infected Tax1bp1-/- cells gave rise to significant increases in Mtb colocalization with ubiquitin, phospho-TBK1, and p62 compared to infected wild-type macrophages (Figure 5B), indicating that this receptor functions subsequent to p62 and the assembly of signaling complexes to the phagosome, similar to that observed with Salmonella eneterica (Tumbarello et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on the microscopy data shown in Figure 5B, and is supported by a citation to Tumbarello et al., 2015.

claim: p62-deficient macrophages showed decreased targeting of Mtb to ubiquitin (FK2) compared to wild-type cells.
source: Similar to prior results showing that p62-deficient macrophages are impaired in the targeting of Shigella vacuolar remnants to ubiquitin (Dupont et al., 2009), we found decreased targeting of Mtb to ubiquitin (FK2) in p62-/- macrophages compared to wild-type cells, consistent with an early role for p62 in signal amplification required for full cargo ubiquitylation (Figure 5B; Peng et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on the microscopy data shown in Figure 5B, and is supported by citations to Dupont et al., 2009 and Peng et al., 2017.

claim: Infected Tax1bp1 edited macrophages displayed increased Mtb colocalization with ubiquitin, phospho-TBK1, and p62 compared to macrophages transduced with scramble control guides.
source: In concordance with our observations in cells harvested from Tax1bp1-/- knockout mice, infected Tax1bp1 edited macrophages displayed increased Mtb colocalization with ubiquitin, phospho-TBK1, and p62 compared to macrophages transduced with scramble control guides (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Tax1bp1 edited or targeted knockout macrophages, a slight yet significant decrease in colocalization with LC3 was observed during Mtb infection.
source: However, during Mtb infection of Tax1bp1 edited or targeted knockout macrophages, we observed a slight yet significant decrease in colocalization with LC3 (Figure 6A and B) that persisted in the presence of interferon-γ (IFN-γ) stimulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the microscopy data shown in Figure 6A, 6B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAX1BP1 is required for efficient delivery of LC3-containing autophagosomal membranes to the Mtb containing phagosome.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that TAX1BP1 functions in a specific step of autophagosomal targeting and is required for efficient delivery LC3-containing autophagosomal membranes to the Mtb containing phagosome.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the microscopy data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: A moderate yet statistically significant increase in Mtb CFUs was observed at 3- and 5 days post-infection in Tax1bp1-/- macrophages compared to wild-type controls.
source: We observed a moderate yet statistically significant increase in Mtb CFUs at 3- and 5 days post-infection in Tax1bp1-/- macrophages compared to wild-type controls (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is based on the CFU data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Using a bioluminescent Mtb reporter strain at a multiplicity of infection of 2 or 5, bacterial growth was accelerated in Tax1bp1-/- macrophages.
source: Likewise, using a bioluminescent Mtb reporter strain (Roberts et al., 2019) at a multiplicity of infection of 2 or 5, bacterial growth was similarly accelerated in Tax1bp1-/- macrophages (Figure 6D and E; Penn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on the luminescence data shown in Figure 6D and 6E, and is supported by citations to Roberts et al., 2019 and Penn et al., 2018.

claim: Tax1bp1-/- macrophages were still capable of restricting Mtb growth when stimulated with IFN-γ.
source: In contrast, Tax1bp1-/- macrophages were still capable of restricting Mtb growth when stimulated with IFN-γ, an effect likely due to production of normal levels of nitric oxide, the major anti-Mtb effector of murine macrophages induced by this cytokine (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of IFN-γ, TAX1BP1 deficiency leads to increased Mtb growth in macrophages ex vivo.
source: These results reveal that, in the absence of IFN-γ, TAX1BP1 deficiency leads to increased Mtb growth in macrophages ex vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the growth data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: Levels of secreted pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-12, and TNF-α did not significantly change in Tax1bp1-/- macrophages.
source: Although TAX1BP1 regulates NF-κB-mediated inflammation in some contexts (Iha et al., 2008), levels of secreted pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-12, and TNF-α did not significantly change in these experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on the cytokine data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and is supported by a citation to Iha et al., 2008.

claim: A modest yet significant increase in the production of type I interferon was measured in Tax1bp1-/- macrophages, consistent with previous reports of TAX1BP1 action.
source: However, we measured a modest yet significant increase in the production of type I interferon, a cytokine that promotes bacterial growth in vivo, consistent with previous reports of TAX1BP1 action (Parvatiyar et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on the ISRE reporter data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, and is supported by a citation to Parvatiyar et al., 2010.

claim: The study generated a comprehensive database of changes in protein abundance, phosphorylation, and ubiquitylation during Mtb infection of primary bone marrow-derived macrophages.
source: In this study, we generated a comprehensive database of changes in protein abundance, phosphorylation, and ubiquitylation during Mtb infection of primary bone marrow-derived macrophages.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the study's main output.

claim: The thousands of PTM changes identified represent an ensemble of the various pathways that are integrated to meet the challenge of infection, but also reflect the pathogenic strategies of Mtb.
source: We envision that the thousands of PTM changes we have identified represents an ensemble of the various pathways that are integrated to meet the challenge of infection, but also reflect the pathogenic strategies of Mtb.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The analysis revealed changes in macrophage functional pathways not previously known to play a role during infection such as mRNA metabolism and DNA replication.
source: In addition to these host pathways, our analysis also revealed changes in macrophage functional pathways not previously known to play a role during infection such as mRNA metabolism and DNA replication, highlighting potential areas of new biology involved in the host response to Mtb.
evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Autophagy receptor phosphorylation, including TAX1BP1, was greatest between the two peaks of overall host protein phosphorylation (6–8 hr).
source: In contrast to the bimodal peak in overall host protein phosphorylation early (2–4 hr) and late (24 hr) after infection, autophagy receptor phosphorylation, including TAX1BP1, was greatest in between these two peaks (6–8 hr).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2C-G.

claim: Dephosphorylation of two residues in the BH3 domain of BNIP3L (Ser-141 and Ser-144) was found during Mtb infection.
source: We found Mtb infection elicited post-translational modifications in several autophagy receptors including dephosphorylation of two residues in the BH3 domain of BNIP3L (Figure 2B E), an atypical BH3-only protein involved in mitochondrial clearance (Novak et al., 2010) and cell death (Imazu et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2B and 2E, and is supported by citations to Novak et al., 2010 and Imazu et al., 1999.

claim: Novel phosphosites in FUNDC1 (Tyr-11) and Optineurin (Thr-210, Thr-212, and Ser-556) were identified.
source: Our phosphoproteomic analysis also identified new phosphosites in FUNDC1 (Tyr-11) and Optineurin. While affinity purification of GFP-tagged optineurin previously revealed TBK1-mediated phosphorylation at residues adjacent to the LIR and UBAN domains of Optineurin (Richter et al., 2016), we found two novel phosphosites between its LIR and coiled coil domains at Thr-210 and Thr-212, in addition to a phosphosite at Ser-556 in its zinc finger domain (Figure 2B–G).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2B-G, and is supported by a citation to Richter et al., 2016.

claim: p62 protein abundance and ubiquitylation increased during Mtb infection.
source: In addition to undergoing extensive phosphorylation, p62 protein abundance and ubiquitylation increased during Mtb infection (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Supplementary file 4.

claim: A novel ubiquitylation site in the p62 dimerization domain at Lys-13 was discovered during Mtb infection.
source: While ubiquitylation of human p62 at Lys-157 has been previously reported in HEK293T (Peng et al., 2017) and SUMOylation of human p62 at Lys-437 was discovered in HeLa and U2OS cell lines (Hendriks et al., 2017), we discovered a third lysine residue ubiquitylated in the dimerization domain during Mtb infection (Lys-13) which has not been described previously.
evidence: This claim is based on the data from the study, and is supported by citations to Peng et al., 2017 and Hendriks et al., 2017.

claim: p62-deficient macrophages were unable to recruit ubiquitin to Mtb, supporting a model whereby p62 recruitment leads to a feed forward loop with further recruitment of ubiquitin to the autophagosome.
source: Indeed, we found that p62-deficient macrophages were unable to recruit ubiquitin to Mtb, supporting a model whereby p62 recruitment leads to a feed forward loop with further recruitment of ubiquitin to the autophagosome (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 5B and the model shown in Figure 7.

claim: TAX1BP1 was phosphorylated during Mtb infection, and its protein abundance also increased.
source: Finally, the autophagy receptor, TAX1BP1, was phosphorylated during Mtb infection, and its protein abundance also increased (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 4.

claim: TAX1BP1 functions at a step downstream of p62, ubiquitin, and phospho-TBK1 recruitment, enabling full maturation of the ubiquitylated Mtb phagosome to a LC3-positive phagophore.
source: In contrast to p62's function in recruiting ubiquitin to the Mtb autophagosome, TAX1BP1 appears to function at a step downstream of p62, ubiquitin, and phospho-TBK1 recruitment, enabling full maturation of the ubiquitylated Mtb phagosome to a LC3-positive phagophore (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data shown in Figures 5 and 6, and is illustrated in the model shown in Figure 7.

claim: TAX1BP1 is not required for global autophagy in T cells or MEFs.
source: Intriguingly, TAX1BP1 is not required for global autophagy in T cells or MEFs (Whang et al., 2017), indicating that TAX1BP1 may play a role in autophagy of select cargos.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Whang et al., 2017.

claim: TAX1BP1 has been implicated as an autophagy receptor important for clearance of Salmonella in a manner that requires myosin VI.
source: However, TAX1BP1 has been implicated as an autophagy receptor important for clearance of Salmonella in a manner that requires myosin VI, one of TAX1BP1's binding partners (Tumbarello et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tumbarello et al., 2015.

claim: TAX1BP1 was originally identified as an A20-binding protein.
source: Originally identified as an A20-binding protein (Heyninck et al., 1999), TAX1BP1 activates this ubiquitin editing enzyme to downregulate inflammatory responses by inhibiting TNF-α and IL-1β-induced NF-kB activation (Iha et al., 2008; Shembade et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heyninck et al., 1999; Iha et al., 2008; Shembade et al., 2011.

claim: Increased TAX1BP1 phosphorylation at Ser-693, a substrate for IKKα, was identified during infection.
source: Given that hyperinflammatory responses promote Mtb infection (Olive and Sassetti, 2018), we reasoned TAX1BP1 may also function to limit these responses, especially since we identified increased TAX1BP1 phosphorylation at Ser-693, a substrate for IKKα, during infection.
evidence: This claim is based on the data from the study, and is supported by a citation to Olive and Sassetti, 2018.

claim: The mass spectrometry proteomics RAW mass spectrum files and all database searches have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD015361.
source: The mass spectrometry proteomics RAW mass spectrum files and all database searches have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE (Perez-Riverol et al., 2019; Deutsch et al., 2017) partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD015361.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability, supported by citations to Perez-Riverol et al., 2019 and Deutsch et al., 2017.
